title: Automation adjustment: Later employment hides incumbent losses
desc: Uses historical evidence to separate cohort employment recovery from persistent losses in career quality among displaced workers.

kps.k: Automation can preserve employment for later entrants while imposing lasting losses on incumbent workers.
kps.d: Feigenbaum and Gross’s study of U.S. telephone mechanization separates local labor-market adjustment from individual career outcomes. Operator employment among subsequent cohorts of young women fell 50–80%, yet their overall employment rates did not decline. Existing operators experienced persistent displacement. The study therefore challenges both the inference that disappearing occupations necessarily cause lasting aggregate joblessness and the inference that stable employment means workers escaped harm.

qs.q: Our exercise comprises two distinct but closely related analyses, on two samples, answering two questions: (i) how did automating telephone service affect incumbent tele- phone operators and (ii) how did it affect future generations of young women entering the labor market?
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: As a first step, we show that after a city was cut over to mechanical operation, the number of 16 to 25 year old women in subsequent cohorts employed as telephone operators immediately and permanently fell by 50 to 80%.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Replacement employment did not consistently preserve career prospects or job quality.
kps.d: Exposed incumbent operators were about 8 percentage points less likely to remain operators a decade later; those over 25 were roughly 7 points less likely to work at all. Among incumbents still working, occupation scores fell 5%, while untreated peers’ scores rose 8%. These scores measure occupation-level earnings, not individual wage changes. Later cohorts found secretarial and service work, but the youngest more often entered lower-paid services. The inferred loss of entry-level opportunities for 10–15% of peak cohorts measures potential exposure, not additional unemployment.

qs.q: To answer this question we construct occupation scores for women      in 1940 as the median earnings reported among all women in 1940 in each occupation, analogous to how IPUMS      creates occupation scores for the entire population in 1950.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The authors favor new labor demand as the adjustment mechanism, but do not establish it conclusively.
kps.d: Secretarial employment expanded mainly in industries that had not previously employed such workers, which the authors interpret as new task creation consistent with Acemoglu and Restrepo’s theory. They find little support for adjustment through wage cuts, crowding out other demographic groups, or direct telephone-related employment growth. Rate increases and small estimated business time savings also weaken a direct productivity-spillover explanation. However, wage estimates cannot exclude changes of ±10%, and the lunch-counter evidence remains suggestive. Displacement appears stronger in manufacturing-intensive cities and under slack Depression-era demand, making adjustment conditional on opportunities to create replacement work.

qs.q: In addition to evidence inconsistent with other mechanisms, we show that most of the growth in secretarial employment took place in industries which had not previously employed these kinds of workers, which we interpret as evidence of the emergence of new work (Autor et al.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018) predict that in these contexts, firms may endogenously create new uses for labor as old uses get automated, and that this is how employment rates can be sustained even as increasingly more tasks are performed by capital.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Automation redistributed tasks across skill, age and gender groups rather than eliminating all related work.
kps.d: The authors attribute mechanization primarily to the technical demands of expanding telephone networks, rather than labor-market conditions. Machines replaced local switching, while complex long-distance, information and emergency tasks continued to require experienced operators, generally older women. Equipment maintenance increased demand for technicians, predominantly men. Complementary jobs therefore did not necessarily benefit the workers whose tasks disappeared, and related telephone work absorbed only a small share of displaced operators.

qs.q: Drawing on company records and empirical evidence, we find that automation was primarily a response to the technical demands of the growing telephone network, rather than labor market conditions.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Because these were more complex tasks, the residual operating needs required better trained, more experienced operators, who tended to be older.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The historical evidence supports a bounded comparison, not a forecast of AI’s employment effects.
kps.d: The study combines archival adoption records, 1910–1940 census data and genealogical links that follow women through marriage-related name changes. It exploits staggered conversion, principally in cities with at most 100,000 residents, and focuses on young, white, American-born women. Weighting and robustness checks support the findings, but nonrandom linkage, potentially endogenous adoption and some pre-existing employment trends remain qualifications. Decennial observations also limit claims about adjustment speed. The authors explicitly question generalizability from this abrupt, specifically labor-replacing technology. For the AI debate, the practical implication is to track incumbent careers, entry opportunities and replacement-job quality separately from aggregate employment, rather than assume this historical adjustment will recur.

qs.q: Here and in Section 6, we analyze effects on local labor markets with a two-way fixed effects (TWFE) specification, exploiting the staggered adoption of mechanical switching and comparing outcomes before and after each city’s first cutover.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Notwithstanding the evidence above, a remaining concern is that automation may have been en- dogenous to labor market conditions: if tight labor markets both drive cutovers and soften their impacts, this could confound our results.
qs.a: Answering the Call of Automation: How the Labor Market Adjusted to Mechanizing Telephone Operation · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The academia-and-research evidence supports the proposition that aggregate or cohort-level employment adjustment can conceal substantial losses for workers directly displaced by automation. The study’s central analytical distinction is between incumbent telephone operators and later cohorts entering the labour market: later cohorts maintained overall employment despite the collapse of operator opportunities, while incumbents experienced persistent displacement and deterioration in occupational earnings proxies. It also supports the proposition’s emphasis on replacement-job quality, because younger entrants were more likely to move into lower-paid service work rather than equivalent employment. Internal variation concerns mechanism, conditions and generalisability rather than the core finding. The authors interpret expanding secretarial work as evidence of new labour demand, but present that mechanism as suggestive and find poorer adjustment where demand was slack. They also caution that this single, abrupt and specifically labour-replacing historical episode should not be treated as a forecast of AI’s effects. Because this facet contains one curated research source, these conclusions characterise that source rather than academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The source from the 2023–2024 period directly supports the proposition that aggregate or cohort-level employment adjustment can conceal persistent losses for workers displaced by automation. Its historical evidence separates later entrants—whose overall employment rates remained stable despite the collapse of operator jobs—from incumbent operators, who experienced lasting displacement and deterioration in occupational quality. Support is qualified rather than weakened by material internal variation: replacement jobs ranged from similarly paid secretarial work to lower-paid services; the proposed mechanism of newly created labor demand is plausible but not conclusively established; and adjustment was weaker where demand conditions were unfavorable. The source also treats telephone mechanization as a bounded historical comparison, not a forecast that generative AI will produce the same outcomes.
